summary: Describes the observed behavior of the BSD syslog protocol as it was actually used, rather than a design from scratch. It was replaced by RFC 5424.

eli5.summary: It writes down how computers have been sending their diary notes to a log.

questions: what is the syslog message format
subtitle: How computers send event messages across networks

tldr.problem: Systems generate event messages that need to be collected and reviewed by operators, but there was no standard format for transmitting these messages across networks.
tldr.mechanism: The BSD syslog protocol uses UDP port 514 to send event messages from devices to collectors. Each message includes a priority value (combining facility and severity), a timestamp, a hostname, and the event text.
tldr.outcome: Syslog became widely deployed for event logging across diverse operating systems and network devices. However, it was replaced by RFC 5424, which provides a more structured and standardized format.

facts.label: Facility codes
facts.value: 0 to 23 (kernel, user, mail, security, local0-local7, etc.)

facts.label: Severity levels
facts.value: 0 to 7 (emergency, alert, critical, error, warning, notice, informational, debug)

today: RFC 3164 was replaced by RFC 5424, which provides a structured syslog format with better timestamp precision, internationalization support, and optional message authentication. However, the original BSD syslog format defined in RFC 3164 remains widely deployed in legacy systems and network devices.

sections.title: Event Messages and Logging
sections.content:
Operating systems, processes, and applications generate event messages to signal their status or indicate that something significant has occurred. These messages range from routine status updates to urgent warnings about problems. Historically, syslog provided a simple way to collect these messages from devices across a network to centralized collectors, eliminating the need for operators to manually check each device.

The syslog protocol was designed around a fundamental principle of simplicity: no strict coordination is required between transmitters and receivers. A device can start sending messages without any configuration of a receiver, and receivers can accept messages without explicit setup. This simplicity helped syslog become widely accepted and deployed across many operating systems.
sections.eli5: When a computer has something to say—like if it crashed, or if a program stopped—it sends a message. Syslog is the way it sends that message to a central log collector so a person can read it.

sections.title: The Syslog Message Structure
sections.content:
A syslog message has three main parts. The PRI part is a number in angle brackets like <34>, combining a facility code (which system generated it) and a severity level (how serious it is). The priority is calculated by multiplying the facility number by 8 and adding the severity. For example, a kernel message with emergency severity would be <0>.

The HEADER part contains a timestamp in the format Mmm dd hh:mm:ss (like Oct 11 22:14:15) and the hostname or IP address of the sending device. The MSG part contains the program name (TAG) and the actual message text (CONTENT). The entire packet must not exceed 1024 bytes.
sections.eli5: A syslog message is like a postcard: it has the sender's name, when it was sent, which house it came from, and what it says.

sections.title: Devices, Relays, and Collectors
sections.content:
The syslog architecture defines three types of systems. A device originates a message (like a router or server). A relay receives messages and forwards them to another relay or collector, potentially filtering them based on priority. A collector (also called a syslog server) receives messages and stops—it does not forward them further.

The protocol uses UDP on port 514. When a relay receives a message, it checks if the message is properly formatted with a valid PRI and timestamp. If the message is well-formed, the relay forwards it unchanged. If it is malformed, the relay reformats it by adding a valid PRI and timestamp before forwarding. This ensures that all messages reaching a collector have the required fields.
sections.eli5: A device creates a message and sends it to a relay. The relay is like a mail sorting office that can pass it to another relay or to a final collector (a library). Each one reads and checks the message, and passes it on.

sections.title: Security Limitations
sections.content:
The RFC explicitly documents several security concerns with syslog. Because the protocol uses UDP with no authentication mechanism, a receiver cannot verify that a message actually came from the claimed sender—an attacker can forge messages. Additionally, since UDP offers no delivery guarantee, messages can be lost in transit, and an attacker with network access could intercept and discard critical alerts.

The protocol provides no message integrity checking or encryption, so syslog messages sent over an untrusted network can be observed, modified, or deleted by anyone able to sniff the network. The RFC also notes that messages may arrive out of order, and there is no mechanism to detect forwarding loops, where a misconfigured relay sends messages back to themselves. The design assumes messages are sent to trusted collectors within a controlled network.
sections.eli5: Syslog assumes everyone on the network is friendly. Someone mean could pretend to be a computer and send fake messages, or delete real ones, and nobody would notice.

sections.title: Flexibility and Conventions
sections.content:
Although the RFC standardizes the syslog message format, it deliberately leaves much flexibility for implementers. The message content itself has no strict standard—different systems and applications format their messages differently. Devices send event messages using processes like syslogd on Unix systems, which can be configured to route messages to local files, the console, or remote collectors based on the facility and severity.

The RFC documents common conventions that have emerged over time, such as including a process ID in square brackets (like su[123]) or using a colon or bracket to separate the program tag from the message text. However, these are recommendations, not requirements. The protocol's flexibility in accepting various message formats was intentional, allowing it to work with diverse legacy systems and new implementations without requiring strict standardization.
sections.eli5: Each computer can send messages in its own style, and the syslog collector will accept them. It's like a librarian who will file away letters written in different styles as long as they have a date and sender name.

fields.desc: Local time: Mmm dd hh:mm:ss (e.g., Oct 11 22:14:15)

fields.desc: Program or process name (up to 32 characters)

fields.desc: Message text (rest of packet, up to 1024 bytes total)
